comments.content: A call with a duplicate id (already running) is silently dropped. There is no reply and no journal entry, so the server may wait forever. It also hides a protocol violation from the user. Reply with an error Result, or at least journal it as DENIED. Also, `stopAll()` can run between `refusal()` and `putIfAbsent`. A call that arrives after a disconnect then starts anyway and nothing ever cancels it.

`failure.getMessage()` goes straight to the untrusted server. It can be null, which produces "Tool failed: null". It can also contain local absolute paths or other internal details. That contradicts the L12 rule of not distinguishing outside paths from missing ones. Send a fixed generic message to the server. Keep the detail only in the local journal or terminal.

Only `Exception` is caught, and `running.remove` is not in a `finally`. If a tool throws an `Error` (StackOverflowError, OutOfMemoryError, AssertionError, ...), the id stays in `running` forever. Nothing is journaled and no reply is sent, so the server waits indefinitely. `running()` also stays wrong. Put the cleanup and a fallback error reply in a `finally`, or catch `Throwable`. In addition, `journal.call` or `reply.accept` throwing after the tool ran would skip the reply or leave it undelivered.

comments.content: Cancel and completion race. `cancel()` can interrupt the worker after the tool has finished but before `running.remove`. The result is dropped, which is acceptable. But the interrupt flag is left set on the thread while it calls `journal.call`, which may do I/O. An interrupt-sensitive journal or reply sink can then fail. Remove the entry first (atomically deciding the outcome), then clear the interrupt flag with `Thread.interrupted()` before journaling.

`outside()` is a second, approximate re-implementation of the path policy that `AllowedDirs` already enforces, and it runs after the tool has finished. It only looks at the `path` argument. It resolves against `dirs.main()` and falls back to the unresolved path when `toRealPath` fails. It compares against `dirs.all()` without knowing whether those entries are real paths. Symlinks, other argument names, and non-existent paths can therefore be misclassified as DENIED or ERROR in the journal. Have the tools return a typed denial (for example a `LocalResult` flag or reason enum) instead of re-deriving it here.

Only `IllegalArgumentException` and `IOException` are caught here. A `SecurityException` or `UncheckedIOException` from `isRegularFile` would propagate out of `context()` to the connection handler. comments.content: `--allow-read` directories only get an isDirectory check. They are not canonicalized and do not go through `refuseTooBroad`. `--allow-read ~` or `--allow-read /` is accepted and passed into the MXC policy. That gives the sandboxed shell read access to exactly the keys and browser data the broad-directory rule is meant to protect. Apply the same real-path and too-broad check to the read dirs, or document why read roots are exempt.

`refuseTooBroad` resolves the HOME path inside the check for the user's allow dir. If HOME is set but invalid (`InvalidPathException`) or `toRealPath` fails on it, the caller reports REFUSED_ALLOW_UNUSABLE and blames the allow directory for an environment problem. The `isDirectory` check also skips the comparison silently when HOME is wrong. Only direct equality with home is blocked, so `/Users` or `/home` (a parent of home, which exposes every user's data) is accepted. Resolve HOME defensively, and also refuse any directory that is an ancestor of home (`home.startsWith(real)`).

Resource lifecycle: the sandbox (with its temp dir) is opened in `setup()`, but the shutdown hook that closes it is only registered after `summary()` and after the `Calls`/`Journal` construction. If `hello()` or `summary()` throws an unchecked exception, or `Calls`/`Link` construction does, the sandbox is never closed and its temp dir and processes leak. Register the hook as soon as the sandbox exists, or wrap everything after `setup()` in try/finally that closes the sandbox. Also, the hook closes the sandbox while the main thread may still be using it, so `close()` must be idempotent and safe under concurrency.

The event carries only a CommandId, but `end` never compares it with `awaiting.commands()` or `AwaitingAnswer.timer()`. It is registered for ANY_STATE. comments.content: RunState is reset field by field through chained withX calls, and `modelBefore` is then cleared in a second step. Every new per-attempt counter or flag must be added to this list, and the same reset is likely repeated in other steps. Group the per-model-call bookkeeping (retries, overflowRecovered, workRounds, autoCompactionFailed) into one sub-record, for example `CallBudget`, with a single `reset()` method. Likewise, `modelBefore` is a nullable field whose owner is the model switch, so it would fit better inside that sub-record than as a bare nullable on RunState.

The stop reason is only checked on the no-tool-call branch. If the reply stops with MAX_TOKENS and contains tool calls, the last call's JSON arguments are probably truncated, and the kernel still passes them to ToolSteps.start for execution. A tool such as a file write or a shell command could then run with partial input. Check `event.stop() == MAX_TOKENS` before executing the calls. Either drop or fail the incomplete trailing call, or end the run as TRUNCATED. Also, an empty reply (no text and no calls) ends the run silently as completed.

`run.compacting() == null` is used further down as a proxy for "the interrupted call was not a summary call". When `awaited` is false, the code never checks which command was interrupted. A late interrupt from an old model call can therefore append its partial text to a run that has ended and is the latest, even though that call is not the run's current call. If the run later starts compacting, the partial text of a summary call interrupted before `compacting` was set would also be recorded as a reply. Record the command kind on `Awaiting` or on the CallModel/Interrupted pair so this check does not depend on side state.

comments.content: `session.socket` is assigned only after the handshake future completes. `onClose`, `onError`, `stop()` and the watchdog can all call `end()` before that. `end()` then completes `ended` but skips `abort()` because `socket` is null. The WebSocket stays open and leaks. This also happens when `stop()` is called during the handshake: the connection is established and `run()` returns 0 without closing it. `Session.send` also drops the `hello` in that case. Fix: set `socket` in `onOpen(WebSocket)`, which runs before any other callback, and keep this assignment. Then, after the assignment, call `abort()` if `ended.isDone()`. To stop a pending handshake quickly, keep the `CompletableFuture` and cancel it in `stop()`. Note that `Thread.interrupt` on `get()` also leaves the pending future uncancelled.

Failure handling in `send()` is inconsistent. On interrupt the message (a call result or a context reply) is silently dropped. The session is not ended and the server keeps waiting for a result that never arrives. Only the other failures end the session. Also, `get(30s)` is called while holding the lock, so one stuck send blocks all other senders, including call results and cancels, for up to 30s each. When `calls.call(call, this::send)` sends on the WebSocket listener thread, receiving stalls too. On interrupt, end the session (or at least report it). Consider a bounded single-writer queue rather than blocking on a lock.

The `try` covers both `Wire.decode` and `handle(...)`. Any `IllegalArgumentException` thrown inside `calls.call`, `calls.welcome` or `calls.cancel` is reported as an unreadable message (`LINK_UNREADABLE`), and the connection is closed with 1003. Any other `RuntimeException` skips `webSocket.request(1)` and goes to `onError`, which maps it to code 1006. Both cases make the connector reconnect, so a handler bug becomes a reconnect loop with a misleading message. Only wrap `decode` in the catch. Handle exceptions from `handle()` separately so one bad call does not kill the link. Always make sure `request(1)` runs, for example in a `finally`.

`sendClose` is asynchronous and its result is ignored. `end()` then calls `abort()` immediately, so the close frame is probably never sent and the close handshake never completes. Likewise, `onClose` calls `end()`, which aborts the socket before the library can reply to the server's Close. Either drop `sendClose` and only abort, or end the session after the `sendClose` future completes.

comments.content: The verdict is passed from `modifyHandshake` to `onOpen` through `config.getUserProperties()`. That map belongs to the single registered `ServerEndpointConfig`, so every connection shares it (Tomcat and Tyrus both work this way). Two concurrent handshakes can overwrite each other's VERDICT and VERIFIED_AT before `onOpen` reads them. A connection can then be bound to another user's principal, or to a valid verdict when its own token was invalid. That is an authentication mix-up on a path that grants access to a user's computer. The Javadoc on `Handshake` ("this connection's own properties") is wrong. Do the check in a per-request place instead. Options: a servlet filter that verifies the token and rejects with 401 before upgrade, putting the result in a request attribute; or keep only the raw token in a ThreadLocal that `getEndpointInstance` consumes on the same thread. Another option is to read the verdict from `session.getUserProperties()` after open. Rejecting at HTTP level would also avoid opening a socket just to close it.

`verify` and `links.get()` run unguarded inside the handshake. If `LocalLinks` is not built yet (the supplier is lazy by design), or `verify` throws, the upgrade fails with an opaque 500 or NPE. `getEndpointInstance` calls `links.get()` again and can also return a null `links`, which then fails later in `onOpen`. Catch failures in `modifyHandshake` and store an INVALID/unavailable verdict, or reject with 503. Check for null in one place only.

There is a check-then-act race between the hello timer and `attach`. `cancel(false)` does not stop a task that is already running. The timer thread can see `link == null` and close the peer while the container thread is inside `links.attach(...)` or just before it assigns `link`. A link is then attached to a socket that is being closed, and nothing guarantees `dropped()` is called. Use an atomic state (for example an AtomicBoolean `helloDone` claimed with compareAndSet by both the timer and the hello path), or run the timeout and attach under one lock. Also, `verdict`, `peer` and `helloTimer` are plain non-volatile fields written in `onOpen` and read from timer and container threads. `helloTimer` is assigned after `schedule` returns, so the timer could run before it is set. Make the fields volatile or final-like.

`close` is not synchronized with `send` and `ping`. It also does `isOpen()` and then `close()`, which is another check-then-act. Closing concurrently with a blocking `sendText` can throw or produce corrupt frames, depending on the container. The blocking `sendText` and `sendPing` have no send timeout. A stalled client can block while holding the monitor, which starves the heartbeat and every other sender. If that sender is the ping thread, dead peers are never detected. Set a send timeout (for Tomcat, the `org.apache.tomcat.websocket.BLOCKING_SEND_TIMEOUT` user property), or use the async remote with a bounded queue. Have `close` use the same lock, or catch the failure and close.

`onError` only logs at debug level and neither drops the link nor closes the session. Cleanup relies on the container always calling `onClose` after an error, which is not guaranteed for every failure. A dropped link can stay registered as connected. Call `dropLink()` and close the peer here. Logging only the exception class at debug level also hides real failures such as oversized frames.

`lastSeq` has a different error contract from `forEachLine`. `longValueExact()` throws an unchecked `ArithmeticException` for a non-integral or oversized `seq`. Callers (`TailSequence.firstFree`, `TurnQuery.messagesAfter`) only handle `IOException`, so one damaged line can crash sequence allocation or SSE catch-up with a raw runtime exception instead of `SessionCorruptException`. The method also throws `NoSuchFileException` for a missing file, while `forEachLine` returns an empty memo. It skips the header and format checks, so it can disagree with the reader about which seq is last. Map the failure to `SessionCorruptException` with the line number, and decide explicitly what a missing file means.

Only `IllegalArgumentException` and `ArithmeticException` are converted to `SessionCorruptException`. Other runtime failures from `lines.decode` escape as raw exceptions without a line number or file name. Examples are NPE, ClassCast, `DateTimeException`, `NumberFormatException` (a subclass of IAE, so that one is covered) and `NoSuchElementException`. Callers that rely on the corruption contract, such as the inspection tool and restore, will not see it. Catch `RuntimeException` around `decode` and wrap it. This is safe because the wrapper rethrows rather than swallowing.

`Lines.next` doubles its buffer with no upper bound. The same applies to `bytes()`, which casts `(int)(end - begin)`. A garbage file with no newline, or a very long line, causes OOM or a negative or overflowed allocation size instead of a clean corruption error. `lastSeq`, `repairTail` and `lineStart` call `bytes()` with the whole line length. Add a maximum line length, for example a configurable cap, and throw `SessionCorruptException` or `IOException` when it is exceeded. Also check `end - begin <= Integer.MAX_VALUE` in `bytes()`.

`repairTail` truncates with no lock. Readers documented as safe alongside writing (`lastSeq` from `TailSequence` and SSE catch-up, `forEach`) can be inside `bytes()` when the file shrinks. They then fail with `IOException("unexpected end of file")`, which `TailSequence` turns into an `UncheckedIOException`. A second process or another opener of the same session can also cut records that were appended between the size check and `truncate`. Hold an exclusive `FileLock` or an in-process per-session lock across repair and open. Treat a short read in the read-only paths as a torn tail, not an error.

State and the public view advance, and projections are applied, before the result row is handed to Release. If `projections.apply`, `evictor.used` or `release.release` throws, the catch in `onEvent` sets `broken` and calls `processed` (handed=false). Readers have already seen a state with no journal line, and the projection has already applied it. This is tolerable only because the latch stops all later events. It is also true when the journal write fails later: `LaneDispatcher.failed` only sets `halted`, while the view keeps showing the unpersisted state. Suggested direction: run the fallible steps (`projections.apply`) before assigning `state`/`view.publish`. Alternatively, publish the view in the `afterDurable` callback, or roll `state` back to `before` when the handoff fails.

This callback runs on the journal/lane writer thread, not the cleanroom thread. `output.test` and `results.reportDropped` are not guarded, unlike the listener calls. If either throws a RuntimeException, the remaining commands, facts, items and trace records of this step are silently skipped, and the exception goes to the writer thread. The `done` runnable may then never run, which leaks the release permit and the per-user slot. A command that is dropped because the output ring is full is only reported, never retried. Its run is then stuck in a state where it waits for a result that will never come. Suggested direction: guard each command dispatch like the listeners and make sure `done` runs in a finally block. Turn a dropped command into a failure event for the kernel instead of only reporting it.

There are four near-identical overloads of `notifyListener`, all with the same try/catch that swallows the failure. They differ only in parameter lists, so the overload resolution is easy to misread. The fact, item and trace logs omit the seq and session, so a failing listener cannot be traced to an event. A listener that fails after the result is durable (for example the submission-dedup index) leaves the index behind the journal, and the only trace is a log line. Suggested direction: one helper such as `guarded(String what, long seq, Runnable call)`, and decide explicitly which listener failures must trip `broken` (for example the dedup index).

comments.content: A failed history load drops the event and emits LoadFailed only when `envelope.run() == null`. For events that belong to an existing run (answers, tool results, model results), nothing is sent. The run stays waiting, and the late result is lost with no result row. Later events for the same session are processed once the load works again, or are rejected one by one. The dropped event is journaled without a result row, so the next restart treats it like a crash tail and may replay it. This can corrupt a newer run. Suggested direction: notify with the existing run ref and mark the session as unloadable until it is reloaded. Alternatively, treat a load failure as a kernel-visible failure event.

Race in attach(): the welcome is sent before registration, so the peer can close and run `dropped()` in that window. `dropped()` sets `over`, and its `links.remove(principal, this)` does nothing yet. This block then puts the dead link into `links`. Later `dropped()` calls return early, so nothing ever removes it. The dead link also replaces and kills a healthy old link. `status()` reports a connection that does not exist, and `call()` hits a dead peer until the heartbeat notices the missing pong. Checking `over` inside the synchronized block is not enough, because `dropped()` can run right after the check. Check `over` before the put, then check it again after the put and remove the link if it is set. Only replace `old` when the new link is still alive.

The expiry timer is scheduled and assigned to `link.expiry` after the link is registered. If `dropped()` or `revoke()` runs in between, `dropped()` sees `expiry == null` and cannot cancel it. The timer then stays alive until `expiresAt` for a dead link. After assigning it, check `link.over` and cancel the timer if the link is already over.

`verify()` revokes all tokens for a disabled account, but it does not record `revokedAt`, does not take the lock shared with attach() and revoke(), and does not end an existing link. A handshake that already passed verification can still attach. An existing connection stays up until the next heartbeat. Route this through `revoke(principal)` so tokens, `revokedAt` and the live link are handled together. Also, if `accounts.test` throws (for example a DB error), the exception propagates out of the handshake.

That link is not pinged this tick and not revoked. Every tick starts one new thread per link, so a slow predicate piles up threads. Catch the exception, log it and keep the link. Duplicate path can return "accepted" for a submission that is later rejected. `ledger.claim` makes the request visible as a claim before `gate.admit`, `receipts.expect` and `tryPublish` have run. A concurrent retry sees `!isNew()` and calls `receipts.of(...)`. No receipt is pending yet, so it gets an already-completed future and a 200. If the original is then rejected (429/503), `ledger.release` removes the claim and nothing was ever published, so the client believes the submission was saved when it was lost. Fix: register the receipt before or atomically with the claim, or have the duplicate wait until the original is resolved. (1) If `event.apply` (record constructors may validate), `receipts.expect` or `tryPublish` throws, the gate permit, the `newRuns` entry, the pending receipt and the ledger claim all leak. The request's retries are then treated as duplicates forever, and the user's in-flight quota is permanently consumed. (2) `receipts.forget` only removes the map entry and never completes the future. A duplicate that grabbed it through `receipts.of` in the meantime waits forever, so its HTTP request hangs. Wrap the steps after `admit` in try/catch and roll back on any Throwable. Conversely, a stale snapshot can give `needsNewRun=false` after the run has ended, which skips the quota check. Use one source of truth (`sessions.find`) for the ownership and active-run decision. comments.content: The per-user slot taken by `users.take` and the global permit are not protected on the exception paths. (1) If `tryAcquire` throws InterruptedException (shutdown), `giveBack` is skipped. The user's `inFlight` stays incremented and the event is lost without a trace. (2) If `lane(...).offer` throws (for example `Thread.ofVirtual().start` fails), the global permit just acquired and the user slot are both leaked. Each leak shrinks the capacity permanently, and `awaitIdle` can never see all permits free again. (3) When `halted` is set the event is dropped silently. It was already accepted from the input ring and nothing is logged or counted. Wrap the sequence in try/catch: give the user slot back on interrupt, release the permit and the user slot if `offer` fails, and log the drop on halt.

`awaitIdle` can report idle while events are still pending. Events that are still in the input ring have not taken a permit. Events the consumer has passed through `users.take` but not yet through `permits.tryAcquire` hold no permit either. If both parked and permits look free, the method returns true although the consumer is about to admit them. It also uses wall-clock `currentTimeMillis`, so a clock step can make the wait return early or late. Use `System.nanoTime()`. For a correct quiesce, first wait until the input ring is drained (cursor equals the consumer sequence), or count accepted versus released events. In the halted state, parked events are never drained, so this method always spins until the timeout.

Nothing re-triggers it afterwards, so it stays stuck until some unrelated release. Also, a non-fair `Semaphore` with a timed bulk acquire can be starved by a steady stream of single-permit acquires.

comments.content: An unpin at pins==0 is silently ignored. A double unpin, or an unpin on one of the error paths in UserLane, can therefore go undetected. The count can drift, and drift in either direction is dangerous: a count that is too low allows eviction while an event is still in flight, and a count that is too high blocks eviction forever. Log or assert on an unbalanced unpin so a pin leak or double release surfaces.

The retry window is measured with the wall clock (Clock.millis()). An NTP step or manual clock change can cut the refusal short or extend it. In addition, every pin() on an expired FAILED entry returns COLD while the entry stays FAILED, so correctness relies on the single lane thread serializing loads. That is not enforced here and should at least be documented. Use a monotonic time source such as System.nanoTime() behind the injectable clock.

Timeout enforcement has two holes. (1) `open[0]` is a plain array slot written by the caller thread and read by the watchdog thread with no volatile or other happens-before, so the watchdog may see null or a stale value. (2) The watchdog starts before `createStreaming`. If connect or header wait blocks past `firstChunk`, the watchdog sets `expired=true`, calls `closeQuietly` while `open[0]==null` (a no-op) and its thread exits. When `createStreaming` later returns, nothing watches the stream any more. `activity()` only resets a deadline that nobody reads, so `betweenChunks` is never enforced and a stalled stream can hang forever. Use an `AtomicReference<StreamResponse<?>>`. Close the stream right after `open` is set if the watchdog has already expired, or keep the watchdog thread alive until close. Also make sure the SDK request timeout covers the connect phase.

comments.content: Failure classification is incomplete and ordered badly. (a) `AnthropicServiceException` is handled first and never checks `watchdog.expired()` or `isInterrupt`. A watchdog or cancel close that surfaces as a service exception is reported as an HTTP failure instead of TIMEOUT or Interrupted. (b) For an error event received mid-stream, the status code may not be a real 4xx or 5xx. `ModelFailures.http` then maps anything below 500 and not 429 to a non-retryable INVALID_REQUEST. Partial text is also passed to the overflow matcher by message only, which is fine, but a status below 400 should not be classified at all. (c) Other SDK failures, such as `AnthropicInvalidDataException` for malformed or partial events and `AnthropicRetryableException`, are rethrown (`throw failure`). That propagates an unchecked exception out of the model call instead of returning a `Failed` outcome, so the kernel never sees a failure event. Move the interrupt and watchdog checks ahead of the service-exception branch. Map other `AnthropicException` types to CONNECTION_ERROR or a protocol failure.

It is replayed as assistant text and the signature is lost, so the next request fails validation or leaks reasoning into the visible content. A lone `input_json_delta` becomes a text block holding raw JSON, so the tool call is dropped and `stop_reason=tool_use` has no call to run. Pick the block kind from the delta type (thinking/signature → thinking, inputJson → tool_use). Otherwise treat a delta for an unknown index as a protocol error (Failed) rather than silently changing the content. The inline comment justifies this as tolerance, but it corrupts history that must be append-only and signature-exact.

The thinking block is rebuilt from accumulated deltas. If no signature_delta arrived (cut stream, stop_reason max_tokens inside thinking, or omitted thinking display), a block with an empty signature is stored and sent back. The API rejects an empty or invalid signature with 400, so the session is stuck failing on every later turn, because history is append-only. Drop or flag a thinking block whose signature is empty. comments.content: `open[0]` is written by the calling thread and read by the watchdog's virtual thread through a plain array slot (no volatile or other publication). The watchdog also fires only once. If the first-chunk deadline passes while `http.send()` is still returning, or just after the headers arrive but before `open[0] = response.body()`, `closeQuietly` sees null and does nothing. The watchdog thread then exits with `expired=true`, and the `readLine()` loop has no timeout from then on. A server that sends headers late and then stalls hangs the call forever. Use an AtomicReference/volatile holder and have the watchdog close the stream when it is published after expiry (or check `watchdog.expired()` right after `send` returns). Alternatively, make `onExpire` retry until the stream is closed.

comments.content: Streaming robustness: an in-stream error chunk (`{"error":{...}}`, which OpenAI-compatible servers and proxies send after a 200) is not recognised. It has no `choices`, so it is skipped by `continue`. The call then ends as the generic retryable 'stream ended early', or with a truncated Replied if a finish_reason had arrived. The real error (context overflow, rate limit, invalid request) is lost and the call is retried blindly. Detect a top-level `error` and route it through `ModelFailures.http`/overflow classification with a sensible status. A non-JSON `data:` line is also reported as a retryable connection error, which can loop on a persistent proxy message.

A missing `index` becomes 0 (`path("index").asInt()`), so providers that omit it, or that send each parallel call whole with a new id, get all calls merged into one fragment. The arguments are concatenated into invalid JSON and the names overwritten. When `id` is present and differs from the current entry's id, start a new ToolFragments. Also, `chunks.onToolInput(piece)` fires with empty strings for chunks that carry no arguments.

The upstream error body (up to 4 KB) is passed unsanitised into `detail`, which flows to logs, SSE and the journal. Providers and proxies often echo request fragments (prompt text, model names, sometimes keys or URLs) in 400 responses. Redact or shorten it before it leaves the client, and do not persist the raw body to the journal. In addition, `new String(head, UTF_8)` can cut a multi-byte character at the 4096-byte boundary. The overflow classification also receives this arbitrary body, so a 400 that merely mentions 'context' or 'tokens' (for example an invalid `max_tokens`) can be misclassified as CONTEXT_OVERFLOW. Check `OverflowRules` for status plus structured error code matching.

comments.content: drain()/process() have no catch-all or finally. Any unchecked exception or Error (from residency.pin, residency.failure, exit.publish, loader, or an Error thrown by afterDurable or done) kills the virtual thread while `running` is still true. enqueue() then never starts a new thread, so this user's lane is dead until restart. Pins, ring permits and done callbacks for the in-flight batch leak. Wrap process() in try/catch Throwable. On failure, call exit.failed, unpin and discard the batch, run done() for the released steps, and reset `running` under the lock (or keep draining) so the lane cannot get stuck.

The pin loop runs outside the try block. If pin() throws on the Nth event, the first N-1 pins are never unpinned and the permits for the batch are never returned through exit.discarded. Pin inside the guarded region, or track how many pins were taken and release them on failure.

Only RuntimeException is caught. If afterDurable throws an Error, the finally runs done() for that step only. The remaining released steps, which are already durable, never get afterDurable or done, and the lane thread dies. Their commands, pushes and indexes are lost until restart. Also, a RuntimeException from done() inside finally would skip the rest. Guard each callback separately and make sure all steps are processed. Also note that swallowing a failed afterDurable means a durable step's command is silently never released; consider exit.failed or a retry.

A failed write is handled as all-or-nothing. Sessions are written in parallel, so other sessions' lines may already be fsynced. Their afterDurable callbacks are skipped and only done() runs, so durable steps never get their commands, pushes or index updates. The process halts, but after restart the journal contains steps whose effects were never released, which relies on replay to recover them. This is acceptable only if recovery re-releases them. Please verify that, or run afterDurable for the sessions that did succeed. Also, `catch (Exception | Error)` swallows OOM/StackOverflow into a normal failure path instead of letting them propagate, and done() callbacks run without a guard.

exit.publish is assumed to return false on refusal, but a thrown exception is not handled. In that case the current and remaining envelopes are never unpinned or discarded, so permits and pins leak. Also, `usage` is handed only to the first envelope and `usageLoaded` is already true, so if that first publish is refused the usage snapshot is lost for good (the process halts, but a halted-then-retried path would see zero usage). Wrap the publish loop in try/catch and release the remaining envelopes on any failure.

Interrupt handling: the interrupt flag is restored, but the lane keeps running. Every later blocking load or write on this thread then fails immediately. An interrupt is logged as an ordinary usage failure, and quota hooks run with under-counted usage (a quota bypass window). In loadOne (below) an interrupt is recorded as a session load failure (residency.fail, a Failed load) and the session is refused and retried. Treat InterruptedException as a lane shutdown: stop draining, discard the batch, and do not mark the session failed. Do not catch Error here.

The cold-session load runs synchronously on the lane thread, so a slow disk read for one session delays all of this user's events and released-step writes. comments.content: drain() commits the state (a permit taken, the event polled, `parked` decremented, `inFlight` incremented) before calling `admit.admit(head)`. admit goes to `UserLane.offer`, which can start a virtual thread and can throw, for example on an OOM or a thread-start failure. If it throws, the global permit and the user slot leak and the event is lost. The exception also escapes released(), so the other parked users are never drained. Roll back in a catch block (`permits.release()`, undo `inFlight`, put the event back at the head, restore `parked`), or hand the event off before changing the counters. In released(), isolate each user's drain with try/catch so one failure cannot stall the rest.

Every released() call, on the cleanroom/release path, walks all of `parkedUsers` and takes each user's lock. The cost is O(parked users) per event. The user whose event was just released is drained twice, because it is still in the set. The iteration order is not FIFO, so when permits are scarce, whichever user the hash set visits first gets them and others can starve. It also does this work even when `tryAcquire` has just failed. Stop the sweep once `permits.availablePermits()==0`. Keep a FIFO queue of parked users, and skip the user who was already drained.

After a halt (journal failure), `giveBack` does not drain, and the events already parked in `waiting` are never admitted or discarded. They never go through `UserLane.discarded`. `parkedCount()` therefore stays above 0 forever. `LaneDispatcher.awaitIdle` spins until its deadline and returns false, which delays shutdown. A fixed set of parked events also stays in memory. Provide a way to flush or discard parked events when halted, and have `parkedCount` ignore them in that state.

`accounts` gets an entry for every Principal and entries are never removed, so memory grows with the number of distinct users over the process lifetime. The `waiting` deque keeps its capacity too. Remove an account when `inFlight==0` and `waiting` is empty. Do the removal under the lock with a retry or a tombstone, so it does not race with take() and drain(). Also, `inFlight--` in released() and giveBack() is unguarded, so an unmatched call makes it negative and silently weakens the cap. Assert or clamp it.

`found.get().state()` is dereferenced here without a null check. A few lines below, the code assumes `state` can be null ("sessions from before this spec have a null model") and guards for it. One of the two is wrong. If `state` can be null, this line throws an NPE and returns 500. If it can't, the later `state == null` checks are dead code that hides the real contract. `runs()` has the same unguarded `state().followUps()` call. Read `state` once, then either drop the null checks or handle null consistently, for example by treating the follow-up count as 0.

The `run` path variable goes straight into `new RunId(run)`, with no format check like the one sessions get through `SESSION_ID`. A blank value (for example `/api/runs/%20`) makes the `RunId` constructor throw IllegalArgumentException. No handler maps it, so the client gets a 500 instead of a 404/400. Add a shared `runId(String)` helper that validates the format (a valid session ID plus `_<digits>`) and returns REQUEST_INVALID or RUN_NOT_FOUND. Use it in both `cancel` and `run`.

The `default` branch reports every unexpected status (for example 500 or 429) with the SESSION_BUSY code and the text "compaction rejected". This misleads clients, who will treat it as a retryable busy state. Use a distinct error code (a compaction-rejected code, or the same one `submit` uses, SUBMISSION_REJECTED). Better still, have `Intake` return a typed result instead of raw HTTP ints.

The client-supplied `requestId` is only checked for blank. Its length and charset are unchecked, and it is persisted as an idempotency key (journal/index). A multi-megabyte or control-character key could bloat journal lines or poison logs. `compact` has the same gap. Validate it with a pattern and length limit, as is done for session IDs, in one shared helper.

`problem()` calls `engine.queries().session(...)`. For a session that isn't resident, this replays the whole journal file from disk. It is called on every submission that carries a model or images, and it runs before the save wait, so it adds to the 10s budget on a cold or slow disk. Similarly, `messages` loads the full transcript and then pages it in memory on every request. Add a lightweight query that returns only the state (toolChangesInHistory and model), and push paging down into the transcript or cold read.

Every non-normal exit leaves the HTTP response open. `emitter.complete()` is only reached when the loop ends normally. On SQLException (for example `stillValid` hitting a locked or unavailable users.db), IOException, IllegalStateException or InterruptedException, `pump` only closes the subscription and returns. The emitter was created with timeout 0, so the connection stays open with no heartbeat and no data. The browser's EventSource never sees EOF, so it never reconnects with Last-Event-ID, and the console silently stops updating. The SQLException case needs no client fault at all: one transient DB error freezes the stream. None of these exits logs anything, so the cause is invisible. Fix: complete the emitter in `finally` (or after the catch blocks). Log SQLException and unexpected IllegalStateException at warn/error. Complete normally rather than with an error so the client reconnects.

Catching IllegalStateException together with IOException silently swallows real programming or state errors. Examples are an IllegalStateException thrown from the hub or the login repository, or a `send` after the response was completed. They are hidden with no log, while other RuntimeExceptions go to completeWithError. Narrow the catch to the container's "response already completed" case, or log it. `completeWithError(failure)` also hands the raw exception to the container's error dispatch. The response is already committed as an event stream, so this adds nothing for the client, and the failure is never logged by this class.

comments.content: Subscription lifecycle is not exception-safe. (1) `subscribe` registers the subscription in the hub first. If `Thread.ofVirtual().start` (or a later step) throws, nobody closes it, and it stays in the hub with a bounded queue until it overflows. Wrap the code after `subscribe` in try/catch and close on failure. (2) A null `login` is not rejected up front. Such a subscription cannot be closed by `closeLogin` (it filters on a non-null login) and only dies at the first heartbeat when `stillValid` returns false. Meanwhile it receives user events for up to one heartbeat. Reject the request (401) before subscribing. The same window exists when a logout happens between authentication and `subscribe`, because `closeLogin` runs before the subscription exists. Run one `stillValid` check right after subscribing.

The heartbeat is used as the revalidation interval and is not validated. A zero or negative `tantalum.sse-heartbeat` makes `nextCheck <= now` on every iteration. The loop then spins at about 1 ms poll granularity, runs a SQLite lookup (`stillValid`, which makes two queries) and sends a keep-alive each time, for every connection. Also, a disablement or password change made from the CLI in another process is only noticed at the next heartbeat. Until then the stream keeps delivering that user's events, up to 15s by default and longer if the property is raised. Validate that the heartbeat is positive (and bounded) at construction. Consider decoupling the revalidation interval from the keep-alive interval.

Password change is three separate non-atomic steps (resetPassword -> restamp -> deleteOthers). `resetPassword` bumps `password_stamp`, which makes every login row stale, including the current one, until `restamp` runs. Concurrent requests from this session (for example an SSE heartbeat) can fail the stamp check in that window and drop the user. If `restamp` or `deleteOthers` throws SQLException, the current session is dead and other sessions may stay valid. The `-1L` fallback also writes a stamp that can never match, so the current login is invalidated. Do the password update, restamp and deletion of other logins in one DB transaction, for example a single `UserStore.changePassword(name, next, currentLogin)`. If the user row is missing, fail instead of using -1.

`deleteOthers` removes the other login rows but does not close those logins' SSE connections through the hub. `logout` and re-login do close them. The old sessions' event streams stay open until the next heartbeat's `stillValid` check, so another device keeps receiving the user's events after the password change. Collect the ids of the removed logins and call `engine.hub().closeLogin` for each, as `logout` does.

The only password policy is non-empty plus a maximum length, so a 1-character password is accepted. `next` may also equal `current`. Add a minimum length (and optionally reject next == current) in a shared place that the CLI user creation path also uses.

comments.content: `MAX_BODY` is checked only after Spring has read the whole body into a String. `/api/auth/login` is unauthenticated (permitAll), and no code in the shell module enforces a request size at the container or filter level. An anonymous client can therefore make the server buffer an arbitrarily large JSON body, so the 'oversized input never reaches Argon2' guarantee does not cover memory. Reject by `request.getContentLengthLong()` before reading, or add a size-limiting filter for `/api/auth/**`. Chunked requests also need a bounded reader. The same applies to `changePassword`.

The logout order is not failure-safe. If `users.logins().delete(login)` throws SQLException, the controller returns 500 before the SecurityContext is cleared and before the Cookie is cleared. The user is left logged in even though they asked to log out, and the SSE connection has already been closed. Clear the context and Cookie in a `finally` block, or do the server-side cleanup after the local clear.

Partial response head is lost on read timeout. `readHead` keeps its bytes in a local `ByteArrayOutputStream`. When `SocketTimeoutException` escapes (the far socket uses POLL_MS = 30s), those bytes are discarded. This loop then calls `readHead` again, which parses the rest of the head as if it were a new one. A slow site that stalls mid-head gets a corrupted or garbled reply, or a bogus 502. Fix: keep the buffer across retries, for example a small `HeadReader` object that holds the accumulated bytes, or `readHead(in, max, buffer)`.

The near socket keeps `SO_TIMEOUT = HEAD_TIMEOUT_MS` (10s) while `copy()` reads the request body. A client that pauses more than 10 seconds mid-upload gets a `SocketTimeoutException`. `handle` swallows it as an `IOException`, so the client gets no response at all. The 10-minute / 5-minute watchdog never gets to apply. Fix: before `copy`, set the near timeout to POLL_MS and let the watchdog enforce the limits. Alternatively, catch the timeout and reply with 408.

The head timeout is per read, not total. A client that sends one byte every 9 seconds can hold a slot for up to 16 KB x 9 s (about 40 hours). Slow-loris clients can exhaust all 512 slots, and the semaphore is the only protection. Fix: enforce an overall deadline for reading the head, for example by checking elapsed time inside `readHead`, or by starting the watchdog before the head read.

Race with `close()`. Sockets are added to `open` after `close()` may already have iterated `open` and shut down. This happens in `connect()` and in `handle()`. A connection accepted or connected during shutdown survives `close()` and keeps relaying until its idle or lifetime timeout. The 30-minute tunnel lifetime also keeps its slot, so it is never reclaimed. Fix: after `open.add(socket)`, re-check `closed` and close the socket immediately, and do the same in `handle`.

Egress check does not match the real connection when an upstream proxy is used. If local DNS fails, `addresses` becomes empty, and `firstBlocked` has nothing to check. The proxy then resolves and connects to an unchecked address. When the lookup succeeds, the addresses checked are the local ones, not the ones the proxy resolves. This breaks the single-egress guarantee that every resolved address is checked, and DNS rebinding is possible between the local and proxy lookups. If the README accepts this risk, at least apply the host-name and port rules, and make the open-proxy case an explicit opt-in per configuration, not an implicit fallback. Also, `InetAddress.getAllByName` has no timeout, so a stalled resolver pins the connection slot.

### Top Issues

1. **The lane/permit pipeline is not exception-safe, so failures hang requests or leak capacity.**
   - `loop/UserLane.java` catches only `RuntimeException`. An `Error` or an exception from `residency.pin`, `exit.publish` or `afterDurable` kills the virtual thread with `running` still true, and the lane never restarts. Pins taken before a mid-loop failure are never unpinned.
   - `loop/UserPermits.java` commits state before `admit`, and after a halt the parked events are never discarded.
   - `loop/LaneDispatcher.java` skips `giveBack` on interrupt, and `awaitIdle` can report idle while events are pending.
   - `loop/Intake.java` has an incomplete rollback and exposes a claim before the receipt exists.
   - `loop/Receipts.java` never completes futures on `forget()`, halt or shutdown, so HTTP callers wait forever.
   - `loop/Residency.java` has drifting pin counts and FAILED entries that are never evicted.
   - `loop/Cleanroom.java` advances state before the durable hand-off and drops late results with no reply.

2. **Orphaned requests: the other side waits indefinitely when the connector or a handler fails silently.**
   - `tantalum-connect/.../Calls.java` drops duplicate call ids without any reply. It catches only `Exception`, and `running.remove` is not in a `finally`.
   - `tantalum-connect/.../Link.java` drops an interrupted `send()`. The context virtual thread has no error handling. A rejected HTTP handshake (401/403) is retried forever. `sendClose` is immediately followed by `abort()`. `end()` skips `abort()` when `socket` is still null, which leaks the socket.
   - `Cleanroom` drops results for existing runs when a history load fails.

3. **Security gaps, mostly fail-open.**
   - **Filesystem access:** `Main.java` accepts `--allow-read ~` or `/` without canonicalizing it or calling `refuseTooBroad`. `MxcPolicy` denies paths built from non-canonical `user.home`, so symlinks bypass the deny list.
   - **Transport:** `Main.java` sends the connector token over cleartext `ws`/`http` to non-loopback hosts without a warning.
   - **CSRF and proxies:** `auth/SecurityConfig.java` skips the Origin check when the header is absent. Its `sameHost` check breaks behind a proxy.
   - **Logins:** `LoginThrottle` evicts live keys, so an attacker with many source addresses can flush a victim's `a:` counter. `Logins` has no absolute session lifetime. `AuthController` checks `MAX_BODY` only after the body is buffered. There is no minimum password length in `UserStore`, `UsersController` or `AuthController`.
   - **Admin changes:** demoting a user in `UsersController` does not revoke their logins or SSE connections. `AuthController.deleteOthers` does not close other devices' SSE streams.
   - **Outbound network:** `net/Egress.java` is open to slow-loris through a per-read head timeout. It has a close() race, and with an upstream proxy it checks different addresses than the ones actually connected. `net/AddressRules.java` misses embedded-IPv4 forms (NAT64, 6to4) in the own-port guard. It also throws an NPE when `getNetworkInterfaces()` returns null, and it fails open on `SocketException`.
   - **Plugins and shared state:** `PluginGate` swallows hook exceptions (an after-tool redaction hook that throws lets unfiltered output through). It also lets an MCP tool with an unknown server default to enabled. `local/LocalEndpoint.java` passes the handshake verdict through `config.getUserProperties()`, which is shared across all connections. `LocalLinks.verify` does not end an existing link for a disabled account.

4. **Internal exception text leaks to the model, the journal, SSE and the untrusted server.** Exception messages and `toString()` are passed along in `Calls.java` (`getMessage()` to the server, which also produces "Tool failed: null"), `handler/ContextHandler.java`, `handler/ModelHandler.java`, `handler/ToolHandler.java`, `model/OpenAiClient.java` (upstream error bodies and URIs) and `loop/UserLane.java`. They can carry paths, URLs with credentials and request fragments, or be null. Use a fixed message plus the exception class name.

5. **The kernel does not validate stale, duplicate or late events.**
   - `step/CancelSteps.commandDropped` fails the run without checking that the dropped command belongs to the current phase.
   - `step/RetrySteps.timerFired` ignores which timer fired.
   - `step/ToolSteps.toolFinished` does not check slot status, so a replayed event can overwrite a result.
   - `step/CompactSteps` dereferences `compacting()` without a null check.
   - `step/Outcome.enter` builds from a stale snapshot and overwrites newer run changes. `run()` and `session()` return a nullable `Map.get` result, so callers can hit an NPE.
   - `step/ModelSteps` executes tool calls from a MAX_TOKENS reply whose JSON arguments are probably truncated.
   - `step/SubmitSteps` has a single `followUpModel` slot for a whole queue, so a queued message can run with the wrong model.
   - `step/CompactSteps` sets a sticky `autoCompactionFailed` flag even on transient non-failures, which disables auto-compaction for the rest of the run.

6. **Journal durability and integrity are weak, and the journal is append-only, so damage is permanent.**
   - `journal/RecordCodec.java` mutates the memo during encode with no rollback, so a failed append leaves later lines with bad refs. It also rewrites the `UnknownFact` raw node in place.
   - `journal/SessionFile.java` stays usable after a torn write. A failed `create()` leaves a non-empty file with no directory fsync on retry.
   - `journal/EventCodec.java` hard-codes three languages and silently drops new ones. Disabling `FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES` is a global change made for a few legacy rows.
   - `journal/SessionFileReader.java` leaks unchecked exceptions (`ArithmeticException`, `DateTimeException`) to callers that handle only `IOException`. It also has an unbounded line buffer and truncates in `repairTail` without a lock.
   - `boot/Storage.java` treats an SQLite lookup failure as a new request, which breaks idempotency exactly on retry. Its shutdown order is not the reverse of the open order.

7. **Non-atomic multi-step state changes shared across processes (server and CLI on `users.db`).**
   - `auth/UserStore.java` has check-then-act on the last-administrator invariant, on user creation, and in schema migration.
   - `auth/Logins.java` has separate `resetPassword`, `restamp` and `deleteOthers` steps (also in `AuthController.changePassword`). `touch` has no expiry guard. `Logins` and `UserStore` lock different monitors on one JDBC connection.
   - `auth/LoginContextRepository` couples best-effort writes (`touch`, `sweep`) to the login validity path, so a transient SQLite busy error logs users out or blocks login.
   - `web/UsersController` applies `setAdmin`, `disable` and `enable` as separate calls.
   - `PluginSwitches` and `LocalTokens` have inconsistent `busy_timeout` and no WAL mode.

8. **Model clients send requests the API will reject, and handle streams poorly.**
   - `model/ClaudeRequest.java` sends whitespace-only or empty text blocks and empty tool results. It also uses unchecked casts for thinking blocks, a `HashMap` for tool schemas (unstable cache keys), and a raw-byte 32 MB check against a base64-encoded limit.
   - `model/ClaudeClient.java` turns unknown block types into empty text blocks, sends thinking blocks with empty signatures, and produces "refused: null". Its watchdog slot is not volatile and classification is mis-ordered.
   - `model/OpenAiClient.java` never closes the response body, ignores in-stream error chunks, and merges tool calls when `index` is missing. It also replaces invalid arguments with `{}` silently.

9. **Resource leaks on constructor and open failure paths.**
   - `boot/Engine.java` leaves most closeables open and leaves started rings running on a late failure.
   - `local/sandbox/Mxc.java` leaks the temp dir, and its `finally` cleanup is not exception-safe.
   - `PluginSwitches`, `UserStore`, `LocalTokens`, `journal/StoreLock.java` and `browser/UserBrowser.java` leak connections or channels.
   - `Main.java` registers the shutdown hook only after setup is done.

10. **Unbounded growth and wall-clock timing.** Maps that never shrink: `LocalLinks.revokedAt`, `LaneDispatcher` lanes, `UserPermits.accounts`, `ToolHandler` limiters, `RecordMemo`. Wall-clock timing is used in `loop/Evictor.java` and `loop/Residency.java` where a monotonic clock is needed.

### Module Hotspots

- **`tantalum-shell/.../loop/`** (`UserLane`, `UserPermits`, `LaneDispatcher`, `Intake`, `Receipts`, `Residency`, `Evictor`, `Cleanroom`) has the densest cluster of high-severity concurrency findings, all around lifecycle, permit accounting and hangs.
- **`tantalum-shell/.../auth/` and `web/`** (`UserStore`, `Logins`, `LoginContextRepository`, `LoginThrottle`, `SecurityConfig`, `AuthController`, `UsersController`, `EventStreamController`, `ApiController`) cover authentication and session security, atomicity and input validation.
- **`tantalum-shell/.../journal/`** (`RecordCodec`, `RecordMemo`, `SessionFile`, `SessionFileReader`, `EventCodec`, `StoreLock`, `TailSequence`) covers durability and corruption handling, with several unbounded-memory and CPU-growth findings.
- **`tantalum-shell/.../model/`** (`ClaudeRequest`, `ClaudeClient`, `OpenAiClient`) has many correctness bugs that produce repeated 400s.
- **`tantalum-shell/.../local/`** (`LocalEndpoint`, `LocalLinks`, `LocalTokens`) has handshake and link races.
- **`tantalum-shell/.../net/`** (`Egress`, `AddressRules`) covers SSRF and egress-guard bypass.
- **`tantalum-shell/.../browser/`** (`Browsers`, `UserBrowser`) has failure-handling and leak issues.
- **`tantalum-kernel/.../step/`** has stale-event handling and flag-threading problems.
- **`tantalum-connect/`** (`Calls`, `Link`, `Main`) has protocol hangs and sandbox-scope risk.
- **`tantalum-local/.../sandbox/`** (`Mxc`, `MxcPolicy`) has cleanup and policy-canonicalization problems.

### Cross-Cutting Concerns

- **Catch breadth:** many sites catch only `Exception`, `RuntimeException`, `IOException` or `PlaywrightException`, and `Error` or unexpected types escape. Examples: `Calls`, `UserLane`, `Storage`, `Browsers`, `SessionFileReader`, `RecordCodec` decode, `WebFetchTool`.
- **Swallowed or unlogged failures:** `ToolSteps` swallows tool-safety exceptions, `EventStreamController` swallows `IllegalStateException`, and `Browsers` does not log launch failures. `LocalEndpoint.onError` only logs at debug, and `PluginGate` hides hook failures.
- **Interrupt handling:** `ModelHandler` does not restore the interrupt flag, `UserLane` keeps running after an interrupt, `Calls` leaves the flag set across journal I/O, and `Link.send` drops interrupted messages.
- **Unvalidated constructor and config arguments:** `ToolScheduler.maxParallelTools`, `LoginThrottle`, `Evictor.Settings`, `TransitionTable.register`, `MxcPolicy.env`, the SSE heartbeat, and `Intake` `mode` (a String). Unchecked client input: `ApiController` `requestId` and `run`, and `UsersController` field types.
- **Unvalidated timer and command identity:** `RetrySteps`, `CancelSteps`, `ToolSteps`.
- **External spec ids in comments:** L12, M8, W6, C16, "需求 x.y", `ops-hardening-2` and similar appear in `Calls`, `Main`, `CancelSteps`, `ContextSteps`, `SubmitSteps`, `PluginGate`, `LoginContextRepository`, `SecurityConfig`, `Fetcher`, `Cleanroom`, `UserLane` and `AddressRules`. Comments should state the rule itself.
- **Patch-like API shapes and god classes:**
  - Constructor ladders in `ModelHandler` and `OpenAiClient` (`ClaudeClient` already uses a Settings record).
  - Boolean flag threading in `ModelSteps`, `ContextSteps` and `Fetcher`.
  - `Evictor.Settings` carries `loadRetry`, which belongs to `Residency`.
  - `Engine` and `ApiController` are god classes.
  - Triplicated subtype lists in `RecordCodec`, and an `Object`-typed queue in `UserLane`.
  - `PluginGate`'s hand-maintained `HOOK_POINTS` is already stale: it lacks `onAnswer`.
- **Duplicated policy logic:** `Calls.outside()` re-implements `AllowedDirs`, `Main.language()` re-parses `--lang`, and `ClaudeRequest.params()` re-derives what `options()` decided.
- **Check-then-act and visibility problems:** plain-field races in `Link`, `LocalLinks`, `StoreLock`, `Evictor` and `UserBrowser`, and non-volatile `open[0]` in `ClaudeClient` and `OpenAiClient`. `AddressRules` has three unsynchronized volatile cache fields.
- **Hard-coded values that drift:** `WebFetchTool` hard-codes the redirect and character limits in its description, and "showing the first 50,000" is wrong after a surrogate back-off.

### Quick Wins

- Put `running.remove` in a `finally` in `Calls.java`, catch `Throwable`, and always send a reply: an error Result for duplicate ids and a fixed message for tool failures.
- Wrap `UserLane.drain/process` in catch-all and `finally` blocks that unpin, discard and restart the lane. Complete `Receipts` futures exceptionally in `forget()` and on halt.
- Close resources in `catch`/`finally` in `PluginSwitches.open`, `UserStore.open`, `LocalTokens.open`, `StoreLock.acquire`, `Mxc` cleanup and `Engine`. Register the `Main` shutdown hook right after `setup()`.
- Replace `exception.toString()` and `getMessage()` in `ContextHandler`, `ModelHandler`, `ToolHandler`, `OpenAiClient` and `Calls` with a fixed text plus the class name. Truncate `rawArguments()` in `ToolSteps`.
- Run `--allow-read` through canonicalization and `refuseTooBroad` in `Main`, reject non-loopback `ws`/`http` or warn, and canonicalize `user.home` in `MxcPolicy`.
- Reject requests without an Origin header in `SecurityConfig` (or require a custom header). Add a shared minimum password length across `UserStore`, `UsersController` and `AuthController`.
- Add guards in `step/` for command id, timer id and slot status (`CancelSteps`, `RetrySteps`, `ToolSteps`). Add null checks in `CompactSteps` and `Outcome`. Refuse to execute tool calls from a MAX_TOKENS reply.
- Clamp or validate `maxParallelTools` and `round.checked()` in `ToolScheduler`. Validate `LoginThrottle` and `Evictor.Settings` arguments and the SSE heartbeat. Null-check `TransitionTable.register`.
- Skip blank text blocks and use a placeholder for empty tool results in `ClaudeRequest`. Use `LinkedHashMap` for tool schemas. Close the response body in `OpenAiClient`. Make the watchdog slots volatile.
- Handle null `getNetworkInterfaces()` in `AddressRules`. Delete the dead `views` method in `UsersController`. Build the `WebFetchTool` description from constants and report `end` in the truncation message.
- Replace external spec ids in comments with a statement of the rule (start with `Calls`, `Main`, `PluginGate`, `Cleanroom`).
- Move to a monotonic clock (`System.nanoTime`) in `Evictor` and `Residency`. Add eviction for `LocalLinks.revokedAt`, `UserPermits.accounts` and the `LaneDispatcher` lane maps.
